postTitle: Life Events and Your Finances: How to Plan Ahead
topic: The biggest cost of a child is the pay a parent gives up, not the receipts

assumptions.notes: Direct costs: about €763 a month (Destatis, Germany, 2018 survey; Save the Children Spain 2024: €758), so €763 × 12 × 18 = €164,808, shown as €165,000. Petra earns €60,000 gross; after the birth she earns €20,000 for 5 years: €40,000 × 5 = €200,000 gross given up. At 40% tax and social contributions on that top slice: €120,000 take home. On return her pay is 10% lower than it would have been: €6,000 a year for 20 years = €120,000 gross, €72,000 take home. Income shift: €120,000 + €72,000 = €192,000 take home. Pension contributions at 10% of gross pay given up: 10% × €320,000 = €32,000. Income shift with pensions: €224,000. Illustrative; varies by country and person.

barStory.disclosure: Illustrative. 40% tax and social contributions on the pay given up. Varies by country.

Everyone prices the pram. Almost nobody prices the pay.
The biggest cost of a child never shows up on a receipt.

beats.narration: Start with the receipts. Studies in Germany and Spain put a child at about seven hundred and sixty euros a month.
Now the pay. Petra earns sixty thousand a year. After the birth, she takes a role paying twenty thousand, for five years.
That pay comes off the top of her income, where tax is highest. After forty percent, she loses a hundred and twenty thousand.
Back at full time, she earns ten percent less than she would have. Over twenty years, another seventy two thousand.
A hundred and ninety two thousand. Already more than every receipt.
Add the pension contributions that came with that pay, and it is two hundred and twenty four thousand.
So before a big change, run the pay line too. Pay given up, times the years, times what you keep. Then add the pension.

caption.instagram:
A child costs about a hundred and sixty five thousand euros to eighteen. That is not the biggest number.

Studies in Germany and Spain put direct costs at about €760 a month, around €165,000 to age 18. Petra earns €60,000. After the birth she takes a €20,000 role for five years, then returns at 10% below where she would have been. After 40% tax on that pay, she gives up about €192,000 take home, and about €224,000 counting lost pension contributions.

Run the pay line, not just the expense line: pay given up × years × what you keep after tax, plus the pension.
